Cloudflare (NYSE: NET) stock has gained roughly 280% over the past three years through Nov. 5, 2026. But it could still reward patient investors for one reason: The business remains small compared with the market management is targeting.

Cloudflare helps businesses keep their websites, applications, and networks fast and secure. At its June 9 investor day, management estimated a $238 billion addressable market for 2026, based on Gartner research. That's the potential annual spending in the markets its products serve, not a revenue forecast. Management projects that opportunity will reach $384 billion by 2029.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Against that backdrop, Cloudflare expects its full-year 2026 revenue to be nearly $3 billion -- representing only about 1% of the addressable market. It doesn't need to dominate every market it serves to become a much larger business. Winning even a modest share of that spending could support years of growth.

Image source: Getty Images.
Priced for growth, but still early

Cloudflare is growing rapidly. Third-quarter revenue grew 39% year over year to $783 million -- its fastest growth in nearly four years. Management expects fourth-quarter revenue to be up about 38% year over year, indicating strong momentum heading into 2027.

The stock is priced for growth, trading at 34 times trailing sales as of Nov. 5. Companies operating in an expanding market and growing revenue rapidly are usually worth holding at a premium. With just a tiny fraction of its opportunity captured, it's not too late to buy the stock. It looks more like a company in the early stages of growth than one nearing maturity.

With so much of the story tied to rapid revenue expansion, the key issue for you as an investor is whether the current valuation can be explained by its sales power alone.

Cloudflare shares are up 326.0% over the past three years. This puts real pressure on the question of how much sales strength is already reflected in the price.

Stronger recent revenue growth linked to demand for artificial intelligence related services and cloud security may support expectations for higher sales over time. This directly feeds into how rich a sales based multiple investors are willing to pay.

Has Cloudflare Run Too Far on Sales?

P/S is useful for Cloudflare because investors focus heavily on its ability to grow revenue rather than current earnings. On this yardstick, the stock trades at a P/S of 35.2x, far above the IT sector average of 2.2x and a wide premium to closer peers on about 11.6x. That kind of gap indicates buyers are paying a high price for each dollar of Cloudflare sales relative to both the broader industry and more comparable businesses.

The fair P/S that falls out of Simply Wall St's model, which blends Cloudflare specific factors like growth, margins, scale and risk, sits meaningfully below the current 35.2x level. Cloudflare CEO: "Cloudflare Isn't a Neocloud." Maybe That's Why Its Stock Soared as Neoclouds Sank ©@metamorworks from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Cloudflare shares jumped 11% after third-quarter revenue rose 39% to $782.5 million. The same week, CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN sank on fears that new rules would limit data center construction.

CEO Matthew Prince called Cloudflare the "first agentic cloud," and its results back up the idea that it can grow with AI agent traffic on a network it already runs.

Quarterly free cash flow has more than doubled since late 2024, and management now expects GAAP profitability in the fourth quarter.

The stock still trades well above its usual forward earnings multiple, so a slowdown in agent traffic would hit it hard.

Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) shares soared 11% today after a blowout third quarter, while CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) and the rest of the neoclouds kept sinking.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, and investors worried they'd push harder to curb data center construction. CoreWeave fell 10% on Wednesday to a new 52-week low. By Thursday, CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN had each lost more than 10% since the vote. Cloudflare sank 8% right along with them ahead of its report.

Then, on Thursday's third-quarter call, CEO Matthew Prince drew the line himself:

"Cloudflare isn't a neo cloud. We're also not, as some of you have called us, the fourth public cloud. We're something different. We're the first agentic cloud"

Judging by today's jump, investors are buying it.

TIKR tracks 34 analysts on Cloudflare. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Cloudflare, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Cloudflare's Analyst Ratings

Agents are moving onto its network

Prince's case starts with how Cloudflare runs code. He said hyperscalers and neoclouds were built around containers. Cloudflare runs on what it calls isolates instead, a lighter way to run many customers' programs on the same machine. He argued that this lets it "scale densely with a level of efficiency no hyperscaler or neo cloud can match."

That efficiency matters because Prince expects agent traffic to dwarf human traffic online, by 1,000 to 1 within five years. He made that call last quarter, and now says he'd "take the under on the timing of that bet."

And the traffic is already showing up. Prince cited third-party data: "between July 1 and today, we added approximately 5% of the entire web to Cloudflare. That's wild." More than 10 million developers were on its platform by October, up from 4.5 million at the end of 2025.
